entry.title: King Crimson Co-Founder Michael Giles Dies at 84
entry.summary: The drummer played an essential role in the recording of In the Court of the Crimson King
entry.content:
King Crimson founding drummer Michael Giles died on Monday, his record label DGM shared today in a blog post. The label did not share a cause of death. Giles was 84. Pitchfork has reached out to DGM for a statement.

Giles first collaborate with his future King Crimson bandmate Robert Fripp in 1967, when they formed the psych-pop trio Giles, Giles, and Fripp with Michael’s brother, Peter. The group released only one album, 1968’s The Cheerful Insanity of Giles, Giles and Fripp, before Peter quit the same year to become a solicitor’s clerk. Still, it set the table for Fripp and Michael’s continued collaboration as King Crimson, the prog rock outfit they established in 1969 with the Gods’ bassist Greg Lake and multi-instrumentalist Ian McDonald. Within months, the group had found a fan in Jimi Hendrix and opened for the Rolling Stones. But it was their debut, In the Court of the Crimson King, that truly cemented the band in rock history.

Released in 1969, In the Court of the Crimson King remains a high watermark and enduring reference point in prog. Writing for Pitchfork in 2019, Ryan Reed said the album“marks a vast fault line in the geology of rock music, refining a nascent genre into a pinnacle of the progressive rock form. The Moody Blues’ symphonic grandeur, Brian Wilson’s expansive production, the psychedelic experiments of Pink Floyd and the Beatles—these are some of prog’s essential building blocks. But with their first record, King Crimson shaped those pieces into a monument, wielding a sorcery unduplicated in the five decades since."

Although Michael left King Crimson in 1969, during a U.S. tour in support of their debut, he returned as a session musician on their second album, 1970’s In the Wake of Poseidon. (Over the years, he would also serve as a session player for Steve Winwood, Bryan Ferry, Yvonne Elliman, Neil Sedaka, and more.) The same year, he also released the record McDonald and Giles with his former King Crimson bandmate. Michael shared two solo albums during his life: Progress, which was recorded in 1978 but not released until 2002, and Ghost Dance, a 1995 soundtrack to the Ken McMullen film of the same name Michael recorded with Jamie Muir and David Cunningham. In 2002, he also co-founded the King Crimson alumnus group the 21st Century Schizoid Band.

“Michael was instrumental in establishing King Crimson as one of the most innovative and influential bands in the history of progressive music,” DGM’s statement read. “His extraordinary rhythmic imagination, musical sensitivity and highly inventive approach to drumming were fundamental to the band's pioneering sound.”

Read about In the Court of the Crimson King at No. 56 in The 200 Best Albums of the 1960s.

entry.title: Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Dies at 65
entry.summary: The guitarist was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018
entry.content:
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, who co-wrote hits like “Girls on Film” and “Hungry Like the Wolf,” died at home on Monday of prostate cancer. The band confirmed the news in a joint statement with his wife, Tracey, shared to their website. He was 65. Pitchfork has reached out to Duran Duran’s representatives for comment.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the band wrote. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”

Taylor joined Duran Duran in 1980, shortly after the band had begun booking live gigs at Birmingham club the Rum Runner. He had encountered the band’s ad in Melody Maker for a “live-wire guitarist.” When he arrived at the audition he met Nick Rhodes, bassist John Taylor, and drummer Roger Taylor, recounting in his 2008 memoir Wild Boy, “The three of us had a good laugh about the fact that by coincidence we all shared the same surname.” Le Bon rounded out the lineup just a few months later, and the band signed to EMI Records in December, dropping their debut single “Planet Earth” in 1981.

The next two years saw Duran Duran become one of American MTV’s first success stories. The channel’s consistent airing of the videos for “Hungry Like the Wolf” and “Rio”—both of which Taylor co-wrote—earned the ban a massive fanbase oversees, with some calling them the leaders of a “Second British Invasion." They shared their third album, Seven and the Ragged Tiger, in 1983.

By 1984, a rift had emerged in Duran Duran, leading Andy and his bandmate John to form a new group, Power Station, with Robert Palmer and Chic drummer Tony Thompson. Although the supergroup didn’t last long, they recorded with Rod Stewart, Belinda Carlisle, and other big names during their active period. Duran Duran reunited in 1985 to perform at Live Aid in Philadelphia, but the show proved less of a reunion than a curtain call: Andy quit the band in 1986 to pursue a solo career that spawned two albums: 1987’s Thunder and 1990’s Dangerous. He also released a single, “Love or Liberation,” in 2019.

Although Andy rejoined Duran Duran during their 1993 comeback, the return proved short-lived, and neither John nor Roger took part in it. Andy stuck around for a 2001 reunion tour and the 2004 album Astronaut, but ultimately departed the group for a second time midway through recording an album in 2006. “Perhaps things might have been different if we all sat down together and discussed the tensions that tore us apart the first time around, but that never happened,” he wrote in Wild Boy. “There was no cocaine the second time around, but in the end, it was the similar tensions caused by internal disagreements that came bubbling back to the surface. History really did repeat itself.”

Andy’s illness was first publicized in 2022 at Duran Duran’s Rock Hall induction, when lead singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from Andy explaining that his absence at the ceremony was due to a diagnosis of stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer he received in 2018. “I'm so very proud of these four brothers; I'm amazed at their durability, and I'm overjoyed at accepting this award,” he wrote of his bandmates. “I often doubted the day would come. I'm sure as hell glad I'm around to see the day.”

entry.title: Bradford Cox Reveals Autism Diagnosis
entry.summary: “I didn’t understand that I was unable to stop talking, that I was in this neurodivergent state”
entry.content:
In his first interview in years, Bradford Cox has shared a pair of significant life updates: that he was diagnosed with autism during the pandemic, and that his beloved dog, Faulkner, died in April this year. Discussing the background of his return as Atlas Sound with new album Thanatos, Cox told The New York Times the diagnosis had shone new light on aspects of his personality. “I didn’t understand that I was unable to stop talking, that I was in this neurodivergent state,” he told Grayson Haver Currin. “It explained my rambling and my sensory obsessions, things that people find charming when they want to and, when they don’t, are annoying.”

Cox appears to have taken the diagnosis in stride. Showing up to his favorite stationery store during the interview, he tells the shopkeeper, “I am in heaven, sir…. On the phone, you were like, ‘Why do people think this is so great?’ I’m autistic, and this is heaven.”

Cox goes on to explain that his revival of Atlas Sound was prompted, in part, by Faulkner’s death. “I thought, ‘What do I have to take care of now? Where do I put my love and attention?’” he said. In August, Cox accepted an offer from Making Time ∞ festival to play his first show in seven years. By that time, he had accumulated more than 1,500 new pieces of music. After the comeback gig, Cox completed Thanatos in late October and urged 4AD to rush its release, lest he change his mind. Faulkner is credited, among the album’s studio personnel, with emotional support.

entry.title: Erykah Badu Does “Breezy,” Salutes Elton John on Fallon
entry.summary: Her rendition of the Alchemist-assisted single interpolated “Bennie and the Jets”
entry.content:
Erykah Badu got into the driving seat for an appearance as the musical guest on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon yesterday, playing her Alchemist collaboration “Breezy.” Sharply dressed in a khaki suit and extravagant silver belt, Badu led a typically charismatic performance that began with a cruise through Fallon’s studio (special effects in this department were limited) before she hopped out and joined the band to the tune of Elton John’s “Bennie and the Jets.” “Shout out to Elton John, New York!” she yelled for good measure. Watch it go down below.

“Breezy” appears on Badu and the Alchemist’s long-teased album Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment, which finally came out in August.

entry.title: Ninajirachi Drops I Love My Computer Remix Album
entry.summary: Wet Leg, Mallrat, Genesis Owusu, and more lend their hands to I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It
entry.content:
Oh, to be a fly on the wall in Ninajirachi’s group chat. The Australian artist has just released a 20-track remix album of her 2025 debut I Love My Computer, complete with reworks from up-and-coming DJs and veteran producers alike. Listen to the whole thing—called I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It—below.

The new record features a few previously-released remixes, including Horsegiiirl’s edit of “Delete,” Underscores’ remix of “It’s You” with Daine, and Dylan Brady’s version of “CSIRAC.” But there’s also plenty of fresh material here: a Cannelle-abetted French version of “Fuck My Computer” appropriately titled “Fuck Mon Ordinateur,” a Wet Leg flip of “London Song” as “Neva Been 2 London,” and Nikki Nair’s take on “ฅ^•ﻌ•^ฅ” among them. Nina even recruited DJ Love, a pioneering figure in the Phillippines-born dance music subgenre budots, to put his own spin on “Delete.”

I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It arrives just a few weeks after Ninajirachi wrapped up a headlining North American tour. Back in July, she also got the opportunity to collab with one of her self-professed heroes, Porter Robinson. The duo’s song “WannaCry," named for a 2017 global cyberattack, won Best Dance/Electronic Release at Australia’s ARIA Awards last week.

Read about I Love My Computer at No. 22 in The 30 Best Pop Albums of 2025.

entry.title: Tidal Bans AI Songs
entry.summary: In a first-of-its-kind move, the platform plans to delete some 29 million songs it deems wholly AI-generated
entry.content:
Tidal is the first subscription streaming platform to ban songs wholly generated by artificial intelligence. The company has announced plans to remove some 29 million songs identified as such on December 9; from then on, it intends to automatically reject the output of song generators like Suno and Lyria, amounting to more than 80 thousand tracks per day. A company statement cited eye-watering data from regulation efforts. In the past 90 days, 43 percent of Tidal uploads were detected as wholly AI-generated. Of those songs, 96 percent have received zero streams.

Tidal’s detection software is supplied by ⁠a French company called Ircam Amplify, which advertises 99 percent accuracy with a 1 percent rate of false positives. By that metric, somewhere close to 290,000 songs will be mistakenly pulled from the platform in the cull on December 9. Pitchfork has emailed Tidal to determine what recourse will be provided for artists whose music is falsely flagged as AI.

The move follows Tidal’s June rollout of plans to tag and demonitize music that is “wholly or substantially generated by generative artificial intelligence.” The new statement, conversely, refers only to music that is entirely AI-generated. Pitchfork has asked for clarity on whether Tidal will continue to demonetize music that is substantially, but not wholly, made with AI. The platform says it has so far removed 65,000 tracks flagged for impersonating artists.

Back in January, Bandcamp became the first major streaming service to wholly ban AI-generated music. Apple Music, and to a lesser degree Spotify, have publicized plans to tag, but not demonetize, some forms of AI-generated music.

Is This Song AI? Real Artists Might Want to Keep You Guessing

entry.title: Hear Clairo Cover MF Doom With El Michels Affair
entry.summary: Leon Michels & co. enlisted the singer-songwriter to recreate the hook on 2002’s “Lavender Buds”
entry.content:
Maybe she’s this generation’s Teena Marie after all; Clairo lends vocals to one of two new MF DOOM covers from the El Michels Affair. She handles the hook (lifted from the Blackbyrds’ “April Showers”) on “Lavender Buds,” a cut off DOOM’s 2004 beat tape Special Herbs, Vol. 5 & 6, released under his Metal Fingers production alias. Hear that below, plus Leon Michels & co.’s take on “Nettle Leaves,” from an earlier entry in the same series.

Since independently releasing her last album, 2024’s Charm, Clairo has found a new label home at Atlantic Records. Earlier this year she linked back up with Rostam, who co-helmed her 2019 debut Immunity, for a single from the producer’s new LP, American Stories.

Read about MF DOOM’s 1999 masterpiece Operation Doomsday at No. 19 in The 100 Best Rap Albums of All Time.

entry.title: Phoebe Bridgers Sets More Planetarium Listening Parties for Lost Weekend
entry.summary: Stargazers of North America, Europe, and Australasia, unite
entry.content:
In August, Phoebe Bridgers launched Lost Weekend with a series of planetarium listening parties. The stars have aligned once more: New dates spanning North America, Europe, and Australasia comprise a second leg of the series, taking place from November 30 through December 13. An Instagram post from Bridgers lists the participating planetariums, and you can check the full schedule at the Lost Weekend Planetarium Experience website.

The hourlong, camera-free parties pair a Lost Weekend playback with one of two original visual accompaniments: a custom dome show, designed by night-sky photographer Babak Tafreshi, or an immersive laser show designed by Laser Fantasy. Bridgers herself is extending her own tour well into 2027, too.

entry.title: Travis Scott, Slayyyter, the Dare Feature on Deluxe GTA VI Soundtrack
entry.summary: The new version features 23 more songs, including contributions from Overmono and 21 Savage
entry.content:
The abundant (in a word) Grand Theft Auto VI companion album has morphed into a 57-track behemoth with the surprise release of a deluxe edition. Nearly doubling the length of the original, the 23 new songs include contributions from Travis Scott (“Burn This Shit Down”), Slayyyter (“Internet $tar”), the Dare (“Interesting”), and 21 Savage (“Cookin”). Overmono also lent five original cuts to the release.

Rockstar Games has pulled out all the stops for the sixth entry in their marquee video game series. On top of landing the likes of Bad Bunny, PinkPantheress, and Robyn to host its beloved in-game radio stations, the studio has also managed to source unreleased songs straight from the vaults of Lana Del Rey and D’Angelo.

French electronic duo Justice manned the original score for GTA VI, which will receive a separate release next month, December 11, via Because Music and Ed Banger.

entry.title: Portishead Reportedly Pull Music From Israeli Streaming Services
entry.summary: The band, long aligned with the Palestinian cause, has not commented on the removal
entry.content:
Portishead’s studio albums appear to have been pulled from Apple Music and Spotify in Israel, in a move that No Music for Genocide has claimed as part of its boycott campaign. While the band has yet to issue a statement on the removal, Haaretz reports that Portishead’s music—including the songs on its own YouTube page—vanished from Israeli streaming services earlier this month.

The trio’s members, long vocal in support of Palestine, reunited in September 2025 to pre-record a performance of their song “Roads” for the Together for Palestine fundraising concert in London. That month, Geoff Barrow wrote on Instagram that the band had “desperately wanted to be involved to put our voice to help end the Ongoing Genocide that is taking place right now.” (Before that, their last performance had been for a 2022 War Child benefit concert supporting relief efforts in Ukraine.) As far back as 2018, the band posted on Facebook to advocate for boycotting Israel over its occupation of Palestine.

No Music for Genocide wrote in an Instagram story that Portishead had joined its campaign and that there would be “much more news very soon.” The band’s songs from compilations and other releases remain live, along with Beth Gibbons’ solo albums and Geoff Barrow’s music with Beak>, according to Haaretz. (Pitchfork has been unable to ascertain the availability of Portishead’s music on other streaming services in Israel.) Pitchfork has emailed representatives for the band, Gibbons, and Barrow’s Invada label for comment. The No Music for Genocide campaign has corralled a vast range of artists—including Massive Attack, Björk, and MJ Lenderman—in its bid to geo-block music in Israel since launching last year.

The Together for Palestine Concert Was Gutting but Necessary

entry.title: Listen to D’Angelo’s Posthumous Song “Kamikazi”
entry.summary: The previously unreleased track surfaced in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Worldwide FM radio station
entry.content:
No, you weren’t imagining the singular voice of the late D’Angelo in Grand Theft Auto VI. As previously reported, there’s a treasure trove of new songs and unlikely cameos in Rockstar Games’ long-awaited blockbuster, which came out last week. Tucked away on Worldwide FM, one of its in-game radio stations, is the unreleased D’Angelo song “Kamikazi.” Now that single is finally available on streaming services. Listen to it below.

D’Angelo was no stranger to video-game linkups. Back in 2019, he wrote the song “Unshaken” for Red Dead Redemption 2. He went on to explain that he was a “massive, massive, massive fan” of the franchise, contacted Rockstar Games himself, and visited the company’s New York offices to play it for hours on end.

D’Angelo died from cancer in October 2025. After a lauded run between his debut album, 1995’s Brown Sugar, and its follow-up, 2000’s Voodoo, D’Angelo became a reclusive figure who rarely resurfaced in the public eye. That changed in 2014 when he returned with Black Messiah, his acclaimed album with the Vanguard, and a handful of memorable TV appearances. He hopped on a few more tracks in the years that followed, including “IBTIHAJ” with GZA and Rapsody in 2019, Slingbaum’s “Behoove” with Erykah Badu in early 2020, and Jeymes Samuel’s “I Want You Forever” with Jay-Z for the soundtrack to 2024’s The Book of Clarence.

entry.title: Don Toliver Concert Evacuated After Airborne Substance Released Into Crowd
entry.summary: Fans were reportedly “screaming” and “coughing up blood” at UK arena Co-Op Live
entry.content:
Police ordered the evacuation of the Co-Op Live arena in Manchester, England, last night (November 22), after an “unknown substance” was released into the crowd during a Don Toliver concert, BBC News reports. The airborne substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas, left fans “screaming” and “coughing up blood,” according to attendees who spoke to local reporters. Toliver reportedly played for 30 to 40 minutes before being escorted off stage; some 50 more minutes passed before police declared a “major incident” and emptied the 12,000-capacity venue. Medics assessed more than 80 people for “eye and respiratory symptoms” and one person was hospitalized, ambulance services said.

Emergency workers including a Hazardous Area Response Team have since been deployed to decontaminate the venue. Entrances have been cordoned off, with police and stewards guarding the perimeter and crime scene investigators in white overalls working to establish the nature of the substance, according to the BBC. The ambulance service urged any attendees who have “noticed side-effects or become ill” to seek medical advice. Pitchfork has emailed Toliver’s representatives for comment.

entry.title: Nirosta Steel Shares Alternate Versions of My Skyscraper Tracks
entry.summary: “Grey Boy” and “Boss Trix” now have “Boss Mix” editions
entry.content:
Nirosta Steel has dug back into his archive an emerged with alternate versions of two tracks from My Skyscraper. Newly available on streaming and as a 7" single, the “Boss Mix” editions of “Grey Boy” and “Boss Trix” were recorded between Hong Kong, Taipei, and Bangkok in 2010, and mixed at the Thai capitol’s Boss Tower (hence the name). Listen to both below.

The release is Steven Hall’s second of the month, following the cover of longtime collaborator Arthur Russell’s “The Boy With a Smile” that he contributed to the soundtrack for the A24’s film Club Kid. Since sharing My Skyscraper earlier this year, Hall has stayed busy with his first proper tour, including shows at Pitchfork Paris and London. He’s set to make his Coachella debut next year.

entry.title: Grimes Releases Two New Psy Opera Songs
entry.summary: “Killing God With Computers” and the A.I.-assisted “Deepseek” both appear on Psy Opera
entry.content:
When she’s not beseeching her ex-boyfriend to pay some respect to his A.I. “sex slave,” Grimes is gearing up to release her new A.I.-themed album, Psy Opera. To that end, two extremely Grimesian new songs: “Deepseek” and “Killing God With Computers.” The former is the only track on the LP to actually use artificial intelligence, according to Grimes, who adapted an A.I. poem made using the titular large language model in writing the song. “Killing God With Computers,” meanwhile, is regular old tech-boosting Grimes.

“While writing [“Deepseek”] and reflecting on the A.I. poem, I realized A.I. feels like how women feel on the internet,” Grimes said in a statement. “I cried while writing it. I felt so strongly how people don’t want me to think. It really is like what it is being a woman.”

The self-released Miss Anthropocene follow-up, which does not yet have a release date, is also set to feature recent single “Accelerando.” Grimes co-wrote and co-produced both that song and the new ones with longtime collaborator Vadakin.

entry.title: Lana Del Rey’s “Crazy for You” Gets Official Release for GTA VI
entry.summary: The keenly awaited loosie has found a home on the blockbuster game’s soundtrack
entry.content:
After floating around as a demo for years, Lana Del Rey’s “Crazy for You” has finally materialized in its final, studio-sheened form on Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album. Now a fixture of Lana lore, the song began to surface, through leaked snippets, in 2022, and one of many rumored complete versions surfaced soon after. Fan speculation intensified this year when the song was registered with a copyright agency, and today, it came out as part of the soundtrack. Listen below.

The year any of these versions were recorded remains unconfirmed. Del Rey’s longtime collaborator Rick Nowels produced the official recording, with Dean Reid and Michael Harris mixing and Randy Merrill handling the master. Several verse lyrics differ between the leaked and final versions.

Having previously proclaimed herself a fan, Del Rey wished her Instagram followers “happy gta day 💕” upon the game’s release. She and husband Jeremy Dufrene also cameo as GTA VI radio hosts alongside Morgan Wallen. As well as the six songs released in September from the likes of Travis Scott, Yung Lean, and PinkPantheress, the soundtrack album features new music from Justice (who also handled the score) and Michael McDonald, Kali Uchis and Helado Negro, Playboi Carti, Dua Lipa, Arca, and Cardi B, as well as the first song in two years from Rina Sawayama.

entry.title: 5 New Albums You Should Listen to Now: Atlas Sound, Toro y Moi, and More
entry.summary: Stream new releases from Atlas Sound, Toro y Moi, and Lorenzo Senni
entry.content:
With so much good music being released all the time, it can be hard to determine what to listen to first. Every week, Pitchfork offers a run-down of significant new releases available on streaming services. This week’s batch includes new albums from Atlas Sound, Toro y Moi, and Lorenzo Senni. Subscribe to Pitchfork’s New Music Friday newsletter to get our recommendations in your inbox every week. (All releases featured here are independently selected by our editors. When you buy something through our affiliate links, however, Pitchfork earns an affiliate commission.)

Atlas Sound: Thanatos [4AD]

Bradford Cox is worth waiting for. It’s been 15 years since we got an Atlas Sound project from the Deerhunter mastermind. Closing out a trilogy that includes 2009’s Logos and 2011’s Parallax, Cox continues to wield his mastery of guitar chug and talkbox vocals, introducing handbells, clock ticks, and güiro to broaden his palette. Complete with a “scent map” recommending aroma pairings for each track, Thanatos shows Cox operating in yet another world of his own.

The time-warping techno producer Donato Dozzy reconnects with his inner child on this double LP inspired by the dubbed Japanese space robots cartoons he revered in the 1970s. He sampled Astro’s title track directly from the series, and the rest of the album embraces more otherworldly possibilities of technology. Dipping from beat-less techno into big-tent trance, the newly nostalgic Dozzy remains as adventurous as ever.

Earlier this month, Chaz Bear quietly posted an album pre-order link to Bandcamp with no description, leaving eagle-eyed digital cratediggers to draw their own conclusion about the new Toro y Moi album. Like its rollout, Unusua leaves things up to interpretation, trading the emo-rap of 2025’s Hole Erth for wandering ambient instrumentals that swap vocals for pedal-to-the-floor piano at largo tempo. A surprise in more ways than one, the songs reveal an artist who, after 15-plus years in the spotlight, still has plenty of exploring to do.

Lorenzo Senni: All Ages [Warp]

At first glance, trance and hardcore have little in common. But on Lorenzo Senni’s first album since 2020, the Italian producer posits that the two genres share more synapses than one might expect. He’s not exactly trading his turntables for guitars, but All Ages retrofits stacks of clipped Roland JP-8000 and SH-101 synths to mimic guitar riffs, and brings in Xiu Xiu’s Jamie Stewart for a feature. The album title references the door policies of hardcore shows—and perhaps also a certain revolutionary spirit many a raver shares. “Time feels short in hardcore because it is short,” Senni said in press materials. “That is beautiful and interesting to me because it feels like you are claiming reality back.”

Lambchop: Demoed [Merge]

Some artists cling to their laurels like lifelines, but Lambchop’s Kurt Wagner is more than happy to pass the torch. Case in point: Demoed, a new EP that invites the likes of MJ Lenderman, Alan Sparhawk, Lauren Auder, and More Eaze to cover songs from the alt-country band’s Punching the Clown. Wagner encouraged his handpicked contributors to keep it simple: Think a sketch, not a painting. The resulting collection has the variegated character of a VA compilation, while still sticking nearly and dearly to the stripped-down ethos of Punching the Clown.
